svg.aria-label: Diagram: why hierarchical firewall policies are the one level where a higher rule cannot be overridden from below, and their four rule actions including Layer 7 inspection; why creating a policy and associating it are separate steps and what the atomic swap gives you; how the predefined rules a new policy ships with differ depending on whether the console or the gcloud CLI created it; and what hierarchical policies cannot do plus the two grants needed to associate one
svg.title: Hierarchical firewall policies: precedence between levels, and defaults that depend on your tooling
svg.text: Hierarchical policies are the one level where a higher rule cannot be overridden from below.
Their shipped defaults differ depending on whether you created them in the console or the CLI.
The guarantee, and the four actions
LOWER-LEVEL RULES CANNOT OVERRIDE A RULE FROM A HIGHER PLACE in the resource hierarchy.
Everything else in this block was priority within one level. This is precedence between levels.
Rules associated with the ORGANIZATION are evaluated first, then the first level of FOLDERS.
Actions: allow, deny, goto_next to delegate downward, and apply_security_profile_group,
which forwards matched traffic to a firewall endpoint for Layer 7 inspection and back.
Create and associate are two separate steps
A policy is a CONTAINER. Creating one does not apply anything — rules are not enforced until
the policy is associated with an organization or a folder.
ONE policy per resource. One policy may serve MANY resources, and editing it changes them all.
Swapping a resource’s policy ATOMICALLY swaps every rule applied to the VMs beneath it.
A policy associated with nothing is an unassociated hierarchical firewall policy. Harmless.
The defaults depend on which tool created the policy
CONSOLE adds four groups: goto_next for private IPv4 at priority 1000 and 1001; Google Threat
Intelligence denies for tor-exit-nodes (1002) and known-malicious-ips (1003 and 1004);
geolocation denies for CU, IR, KP, SY, XC and XD (1005); and the immutable bottom.
gcloud CLI or the API adds ONLY the immutable bottom — four goto_next rules you cannot
modify or delete, at priorities 2147483644 to 2147483647.
So the same runbook yields two different security postures. Terraform gets the bare one.
What it cannot do, and who may do it
NO instance tags — targeting is by network or by service account only. #72’s weak option
is simply not offered here. Secure tag keys are supported as source or target.
CANNOT be assigned to projects — organization and folders only. IPv4 or IPv6, not both.
EVENTUALLY CONSISTENT: move a project or folder and it may take a few minutes to apply.
Associating needs TWO grants: orgSecurityResourceAdmin on the target, plus policy admin or user.
A new policy is safe to associate: its predefined rules are lowest-priority and pass traffic
down to lower-level policies and VPC rules, so an empty policy blocks nothing.
The preview roles orgSecurityPolicyAdmin and orgSecurityPolicyUser combined firewall policy
and Cloud Armor permissions; they still work, and Google recommends migrating off them.
